name: Clean Enough: The Synthetic Water Revolution and Its Costs
description: A scientific and investigative documentary examining the synthetic water filtration systems installed across GLMZ's Tier 1-2 zones in the 2170s-2190s, which were publicly presented as humanitarian infrastructure but which, the film argues with documented evidence, were also delivery systems for corponation-approved neurochemical baseline regulators administered without population knowledge or consent. The filmmaker, Osei Tamboli-Vreeland's former research partner Adaora Brandt-Khoury, submitted the film to three licensed distributors before disappearing in 2212; the documentary was released posthumously by an anonymous network.
cultural_impact: The film's central claim — that Shelf neurochemical baselines were deliberately suppressed to reduce social unrest — became one of the foundational grievances of the Shelf rights movement, repeated in protests even by people who have never seen the documentary itself.
story_hooks: A Tier 1 resident who has never consumed the filtered water — relying instead on collected rainwater — notices they feel and think differently than their neighbors in ways they can't quite articulate.
A HelixCorp water infrastructure technician recognized in the film is still alive and working, and someone wants to reach them before the corponation realizes they've been identified.

The documentary includes a chemical formula in the background of one shot — visible for only a few seconds — that a viewer with biochemistry training recognizes as something currently in clinical trials under a different name.
